strengths: Clear motivation and problem formulation: Well-articulated explanation of why RL fails on long reasoning chains (exponential reward sparsity) with intuitive n-step motivating example

Strong synthetic contribution: Chain-of-parities task provides genuine separation result where AdaBack succeeds while SFT, RL, and SFT+RL all fail, with theoretical grounding in learning complexity (degree-3 vs degree-2 parities)

Comprehensive experimental design: Multiple benchmarks, model sizes, initialization strategies, creative OOD variants (Base-7, Tensor-2), pass@k analysis to verify novel solutions, and honest discussion of failure cases
Practical method design: Intuitive approach with minimal hyperparameters, natural integration with GRPO, and simple binary search over supervision ratios
Reproducibility and transparency: Extensive implementation details, appendices with training details, and candid acknowledgment of limitations and failure modes
weaknesses: Modest real-world improvements: MATH improvements only 2.1-2.2pp over SFT+RL; GSM8k 3B actually worse (-2.0pp); gains primarily on 1B models and OOD variants, not in-distribution benchmarks
Complete failure on instruct-tuned models: No benefits on MATH with Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct; severely limits applicability as instruction-tuning becomes standard; inadequate investigation of generality

Fundamental scalability limitations: Authors acknowledge method relies on global moving averages in large-data regimes, undermining core per-sample adaptation; proposed embedding-space solution deferred to future work

Gap between synthetic and real tasks: Chain-of-parities with accumulating structure not representative of diverse mathematical reasoning; requires SFT pretraining for format learning, weakening 'SFT fails' claim

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Threshold τ appears crucial but lacks sensitivity analysis; ad-hoc choices (10% ρ=0 injection, α for EMA) unjustified; different problem types may need different τ values unexplored

Limited baseline comparisons and scope: Only brief R3 comparison; missing recent RL variants and curriculum methods; evaluation only on LLaMA 1B/3B, not larger models; only MATH and GSM8k variants tested
Statistical rigor issues: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; results appear single-run; critical given modest 1-2% improvements

Incomplete analysis: Limited ablations on design choices; no investigation of which problem types benefit most; pass@k improvements modest with sometimes small differences; underdeveloped explanation of base+AdaBack outperforming SFT+AdaBack

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates why standard RL fails on sparse-reward reasoning and proposes an intuitive intermediate approach between SFT and RL
Theoretically grounded synthetic task: The chain-of-parities task is clever and demonstrates a separation result where SFT, RL, and their combination all fail but AdaBack succeeds
Comprehensive experimental scope: Multiple benchmarks (MATH, GSM8k, Base-7, Tensor-2), model sizes (1B-3B), initializations (base and SFT), and pass@k analysis to investigate solution discovery
Clean algorithm design: The adaptive per-sample curriculum via stochastic binary search is simple and requires only a single reward threshold τ
Honest limitation discussion: Clearly identifies that AdaBack provides no benefit on well-pretrained models and explains potential reasons
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements lacking statistical rigor: MATH improves from 17.7% to 19.9% (+2.2 pp) and GSM8k from 72.7% to 73.3% (+0.6 pp) with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run analysis. Differences may be within noise given visible training variance

Fundamental scalability limitation: Paper acknowledges that in large dataset regimes with many unique samples, per-sample adaptation breaks down and relies on global moving averages, directly undermining the core contribution. No experiments demonstrate performance degradation at scale

Severe practical limitation: Method provides zero benefit on well-pretrained Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct models, creating a perverse incentive (more useful for worse models). As models improve, applicability decreases

Weak theory-practice connection: Synthetic task analysis assumes independent parity learning (violated in actual Transformers), requires initial ρ near 1.0 (empirically much lower), yet produces only 0.6-2.2 pp improvements on real tasks

Incomplete ablations and hyperparameter analysis: No sensitivity to threshold τ despite being crucial; no ablation on 10% ρ=0 injection; no justification for format reward rformat=0.1; no comparison of binary search to simpler scheduling alternatives

Questionable evaluation datasets: Base-7 GSM8k drops <1000 of 8500 problems (~1% difference, likely learned via general arithmetic); Tensor-2 concatenates semantically unrelated problems creating artificial tasks not representative of real reasoning

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite visible high variance in curves. Statement about 'averaging over last 5 iterations with increasing reward' in rare cases suggests potential cherry-picking

Failure mode on instruct-tuned models indicates fundamental limitation: Figure 5 shows AdaBack provides no benefit when models have seen pretraining data, limiting real-world applicability precisely when methods are needed most for state-of-the-art models

Limited algorithmic novelty: Curriculum learning with progressive difficulty is well-established; backtracking in RL exists (Salimans & Chen 2018); per-sample adaptive scheduling is not new. Application to LLM reasoning is somewhat incremental

Incomplete experimental analysis: No study of how performance degrades with dataset size; R3 comparison may be unfair (whitespace segmentation handicapped on parity task); pass@k improvements not verified to reflect qualitatively different solution trajectories

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with a concrete example of why exploration in long-horizon reasoning is exponentially hard
Clever synthetic chain-of-parities task providing a theoretical separation result where SFT, RL, and their combination all fail but AdaBack succeeds
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MATH, GSM8k) and novel variants (Base-7, Tensor-2) with different model sizes
Simple and elegant method that removes need for domain-specific delimiters, improving generality over prior work like R3
Insightful pass@k analysis providing evidence that AdaBack expands the solution distribution rather than merely reweighting existing solutions
Honest discussion of failure cases and scalability limitations (e.g., instruct-tuned models, large dataset regimes)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: per-sample adaptation of existing curriculum learning ideas (backtracking, R3); core contribution is incremental rather than fundamental
Modest empirical improvements on canonical benchmarks (2-3 percentage points on MATH and GSM8k), with most substantial gains on OOD variants

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: reward threshold τ is critical but no sensitivity analysis; 10% ρ=0 injection lacks principled justification; claimed non-necessity of stochastic binary search untested
Significant scalability limitation in large dataset regimes: per-sample tracking breaks down and method reverts to global moving averages, undermining main benefit
Insufficient comparison with R3: only appears on synthetic task; no empirical evaluation on MATH/GSM8k limits ability to assess practical advantages claimed
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to mathematical reasoning tasks; generalization to code generation, theorem proving, and other structured reasoning domains unclear
Unexplained counterintuitive results: SFT+AdaBack sometimes underperforms AdaBack on base models (inconsistent across models/tasks), deserving deeper investigation
Incomplete analysis of what enables discovery of 'new reasoning capabilities': pass@k improvements are suggestive but indirect; would benefit from explicit solution novelty analysis
Multiple design choices appear ad-hoc: format rewards, probability thresholds, EMA momentum—together reduce reproducibility and suggest potential brittleness

strengths: Clear problem formulation with well-motivated sparse reward challenge; intuitive illustrative example of exponentially rare rewards (p^n)
Strong synthetic evaluation: chain-of-parities task provides principled separation result where AdaBack succeeds while SFT+RL fails, grounded in learning theory (parity complexity bounds)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (DeepScaleR, MATH, GSM8k) with novel variants (Base-7, Tensor-2) and robustness analysis of τ parameter
Practical per-sample curriculum mechanism using reward-driven binary search requiring minimal hyperparameter tuning; pass@k analysis (Figure 4) demonstrates solution space expansion
Honest and explicit discussion of limitations: identifies failure modes on instruct-tuned models, well-covered datasets, and scalability issues in large dataset regimes
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core idea of curriculum learning via partial supervision exists in backtracking (Salimans & Chen 2018) and R3 (Xi et al. 2024); main contribution is per-sample adaptation, which is incremental

Modest empirical improvements on real benchmarks (2-5pp on MATH/DeepScaleR; GSM8k shows larger gap but SFT+RL already at 36.7%); no statistical significance testing given RL variance; mixed results vs. R3 baseline (underperforms on GSM8k 39.2% vs 41.5%)

Significant gap between synthetic and real-world results: chain-of-parities shows >20× efficiency over R3 but real benchmarks show 2-5pp gains, suggesting limited transfer of theoretical insights to natural language reasoning

Critical practical limitations undermine applicability: (1) large dataset regime requires global moving averages, defeating per-sample adaptation claim; (2) no benefit on instruct-tuned models (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5) which represent practice; (3) only helps when significant exploration needed—but SFT models may already cover most solution space

Incomplete experimental comparisons: no comparison with batch-level curricula (Chen et al. 2025, Shi et al. 2025); limited R3 analysis with speculative explanations for when AdaBack should win; Base-7/Tensor-2 variants are artificial (dropping ~1000 samples, semantically disjoint problems)

Synthetic task concerns: chain-of-parities uses simplified theoretical assumptions (acknowledged in Appendix B), only 1024 examples, unclear scaling; unclear how insights transfer to NLP reasoning where steps are not clearly delineated

Hyperparameter selection appears post-hoc: choice of τ=0.5 to maximize reward variance based on Razin et al. (2024) which addresses PPO not GRPO; limited ablations on binary search vs. alternatives, or on 10% ρ=0 injection heuristic

Missing elements: no confidence intervals despite RL variance; no ablation on mechanism choices; limited analysis of learned supervision trajectories; claims about discovering 'genuinely new reasoning capabilities' overstated given incremental improvements

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear intuition: standard RL fails on long reasoning chains due to exponential sparsity (p^n success probability). The paper articulates this clearly with a simple motivating example.

Synthetic chain-of-parities task provides genuine theoretical validation grounded in parity learning complexity theory (degree-k parities, sample complexity bounds from Abbe et al., Kou et al.). Shows a clear separation where AdaBack succeeds while SFT+RL fails.

Simple and practical algorithm: the adaptive binary search over per-sample supervision ratios is elegant and avoids hand-crafted curriculum schedules. The update rule based on reward thresholds is intuitive.
Comprehensive experimental scope: multiple datasets (DeepScaleR, MATH, GSM8k), model sizes (1B, 3B), initializations (base/SFT), and new variants (Base-7, Tensor-2) for testing generalization.
Pass@k analysis (Figure 4) provides evidence that AdaBack expands solution distribution rather than reweighting, supporting claims about discovering new solutions.
Honest identification of failure cases: clearly acknowledges that AdaBack provides no benefit on instruction-tuned models or datasets seen in pretraining, strengthening credibility.
weaknesses: Modest and marginal empirical improvements on real tasks: GSM8k shows only +0.6% (3B) to +2.5% (1B); MATH shows +1.4% (3B) to +1.7% (1B); DeepScaleR shows +1.5% (3B) to +2.2% (1B). Improvements shrink with model scale and lack error bars/statistical significance testing, making it unclear if gains exceed variance.

Limited novelty over concurrent work (R3, Xi et al. 2024): Core difference is per-sample adaptivity vs. fixed segmentation. R3 actually outperforms AdaBack on GSM8k (41.5% vs. 39.2% for 1B base), and improvements on harder datasets are only 1-2%. The novelty claim is weakly validated empirically.

Severely constrained real-world applicability: Paper demonstrates AdaBack provides zero benefit on instruction-tuned models (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5) or datasets seen during pretraining (Figures 10-11). As models improve and pretraining coverage increases, applicability window closes. This limits impact as an RL improvement method.

Ad-hoc methodological choices undermine principled design: (1) The ρ=0 injection (10% probability) is introduced post-hoc to fix train-test mismatch, suggesting the core method wasn't fully solved; (2) Multiple hidden hyperparameters (τ, α for moving average, 10% injection probability); (3) τ=0.5 chosen to 'maximize reward variance' per Razin et al., which is tuning for gradient stability, not curriculum design.

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite RL's notorious variance. Averaging over 'last 5 checkpoints' smooths noise but doesn't quantify uncertainty. Impossible to assess if reported improvements are statistically significant.

Synthetic task success may not translate to real tasks: Chain-of-parities is a carefully constructed task designed to benefit from curriculum learning. Real mathematical reasoning involves continuous semantic challenge, not discrete exponential drops. Theoretical analysis (Appendix B) relies on simplifying assumptions (treating each step as independent).

Incomplete comparison with R3: R3 uses structure-aware segmentation (newlines in GSM8k) while AdaBack slices at arbitrary points. On tasks with clear structure, R3 wins. Explanations for why AdaBack should be better are speculative. Comparison on chain-of-parities is somewhat unfair (R3 not designed for extreme sparsity).

Missing baselines and ablations: No comparison with other curriculum learning methods (prioritized level replay, reverse curriculum), other sparse-reward solutions (reward shaping, hierarchical RL), or simpler alternatives (extended SFT with curriculum). No analysis of whether 80,000 A100 GPU hours is justified by the improvements.

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing real problem of sparse rewards in long-horizon reasoning tasks
Elegant synthetic task (chain-of-parities) providing clean separation result between SFT, RL, and AdaBack
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets with new variants (Base-7, Tensor-2) designed to test generalization
Pass@k analysis demonstrating AdaBack expands solution distribution rather than merely reweighting known solutions
Practical method requiring only single hyperparameter (τ) with demonstrated robustness to its choice
Honest discussion of failure cases and scalability limitations enhancing credibility

Per-sample adaptive curriculum eliminating need for manual curriculum staging or global scheduling

Mixed comparison with R3: underperforms on GSM8k where R3 is optimized, wins on harder datasets where R3's fixed slicing struggles
Limited to 1B-3B models; unclear scaling to 7B+ models where most practical reasoning occurs
Acknowledged scalability limitation in large-dataset regime where per-sample tracking relies on global moving averages without experimental mitigation
Ad-hoc implementation details (10% probability ρ=0 injection, global moving average initialization) lacking principled justification
No computational cost comparison with baselines despite per-sample tracking potentially adding overhead
Limited investigation of failure cases; speculation about instruct-tuned model saturation lacks rigorous analysis
Incremental novelty over prior backtracking methods (Salimans & Chen 2018, R3); main contribution is per-sample adaptivity
